media.alt: Smoking is the major cause of lung cancer, heart attacks, chronic bronchitis and strokes

content.text: "Every day, the tobacco industry has to recruit hundreds of people to become smokers to replace the hundreds who die daily as a result of smoking," said Dr Martyn Partridge, Consultant Chest Physician, Whipps Cross Hospital, London. He was speaking at an international seminar on Chest Diseases organised by The Aga Khan University (AKU) in collaboration with the Pakistan Chest Society (Sindh Chapter) from November 2-4.1999 Smoking is just one of the common respiratory problems encountered by a doctor which was discussed at the seminar. Other topics included asthma, tuberculosis and the abuse of antibiotics for treatment of chest diseases.

Dr Javed A. Khan, Associate Professor, Department of Medicine, AK U, noted that "Smoking IS the single largest cause of death all over the world." In Pakistan, at least 54 percent of men and 20 percent of women regularly use some form of tobacco. Smoking is the major cause of lung cancer, heart attacks, chronic bronchitis and strokes. It also lowers resistance to fight colds and allergies. On average, a smoker shortens his or her life by 5 minutes for every cigarette smoked. Nicotene, the main ingredient of tobacco, is more powerful than heroin as an addictive substance. "But it is never too late to quit smoking," as Professor James Friend, University of Aberdeen, encouragingly said. However, the effects of passive smoking are just as dangerous. During an hour in a smoke filled room, a non-smoker inhales the equivalent of 15 filtered cigarettes

"Passive smoking of family members significantly increases the risk of children developing asthma and aggravates the condition of those who already have it," said Dr Naseeruddin Mahmood, Assistant Professor, Department of Paediatrics, AKU. He went on to say that 10 percent of Pakistani children are at risk of developing asthma. Although asthma is not curable, with correct management a sufferer can enjoy a healthy and productive life these include getting rid of anything that is likely to attract a lot of dust such as carpets and stuffed toys. Dr Abdul Majeed Memon , Consultant Pulmonologist, AKU, stressed that it was important to guard against the current under diagnosis of asthma and educate asthmatics "in the management of the disease."

A third common respiratory ailment that received attention was tuberculosis. It is spreading rapidly in Pakistan with over 350,000 active TB patients. An untreated patient can spread the disease to 15 other healthy individuals in a year's time. Dr S. Q. Nizami, Associate Professor and Consultant in Paediatric Infectious Diseases, AKU, highlighted that TB is an "often neglected public health problem with no countrywide data available on the prevalence of this disease in children."

Dr Arif Sarwari, Consultant in Infectious Diseases, AKU, highlighted the over-usage of antibiotics in the treatment of respiratory diseases in Pakistan. He noted that the "onus Iies on both the patient and physician to be restrained, especially in an environment where regulatory controls are lacking."
